analysis.one_liner: Gives immigration enforcement a guaranteed decade of funding, bypassing the yearly budget process.
analysis.headline: The Senate has never voted on the bill; since being placed on the Senate calendar on April 2, 2026, it has sat there with three Republican senators attached and no hearing or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill hands U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) roughly $105 billion in a single lump — $100.4 billion for operations and support and $5 billion for buying land, buildings, and equipment — with the money available through September 30, 2036 [S2][S3]. Normally Congress funds agencies like ICE year by year in an appropriations bill, which is where lawmakers debate the amounts and attach conditions. This bill instead locks in ten years of funding at once, and its text says the money stays available regardless of any law limiting how long appropriations can last [S3]. The bill also directs purchase of up to 3,790 police-type vehicles and funds overseas vetted units [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: ICE gains a decade of guaranteed funding that no future annual budget fight can easily trim. The money flows heavily to contractors: private detention companies, transport vendors, construction firms building new facilities and buying land, and manufacturers supplying thousands of police-type vehicles. Because the appropriation runs for ten years, these companies get a predictable, long-term revenue stream rather than one that must be re-won each year.

how_it_helps.text: Provides $100.4 billion for ICE operations and support and $5 billion for procurement, construction, and improvements, available through fiscal year 2036 [S2][S3].
Funds the purchase or lease of up to 3,790 police-type vehicles and overseas vetted units [S2][S3].
Directs money toward acquiring additional real property and facilities, ongoing maintenance, and facility improvements — long-term contracts for builders and suppliers [S3].
States that the money remains available for obligation notwithstanding any provision of law limiting the period of availability, insulating it from the annual budget process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who cover about $105.4 billion with no offset or funding source specified in the bill. Communities affected by immigration enforcement — including people in detention and their families — bear the policy consequences of a decade of guaranteed enforcement funding that Congress can no longer adjust year to year.

drawbacks.text: A ten-year, single-shot appropriation removes the annual review where Congress examines how an agency is spending, sets conditions, and adjusts the total; the bill even blocks ordinary limits on how long the money can sit available [S3].
The bill specifies no offset — no spending cut or revenue source — so the roughly $105 billion would add to federal deficits unless Congress acts separately [S3].

Funding for 'acquisition of necessary additional real property and facilities' points toward a major expansion of detention capacity, with the details — where facilities go, who runs them, what standards apply — left to the agency rather than to Congress [S3].

Supporters of annual oversight in both parties have historically argued that multi-year funding for enforcement agencies weakens accountability; this bill's rule-of-construction section expressly overrides those limits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: People who back increased immigration enforcement get what they want: sustained, predictable funding without yearly battles. But the way the bill is written trades away the main safeguard Congress has over how that money is used — the annual budget review. Committing roughly $105 billion for ten years at once, with no offset and no yearly conditions, is a poorly designed way to fund any agency, and the decade-long revenue guarantee is worth far more to contractors than the flexibility it takes from future Congresses.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late March 2026, read twice, and placed directly on the Senate calendar without a committee hearing, and no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Eric Schmitt introduced S. 4277 in the Senate on March 27, 2026 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on April 2, 2026 — a fast track that skips committee review, though it guarantees nothing further [S5].
As of the latest action, no hearing, debate, or vote has occurred; the bill sits on the calendar with two cosponsors [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained — the bill has not moved. If it were enacted, ICE and its contractor network would be the clear winners, getting a decade of funding insulated from annual review.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits unvoted

for.name: Sen. Eric Schmitt
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it placed directly on the Senate calendar, bypassing committee.

for.name: Sens. Josh Hawley and Bernie Moreno
for.role: U.S. Senators from Missouri and Ohio; original cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: All three senators attached to the bill are Republicans; no Democrat has cosponsored, and no vote has occurred to reveal where the parties would land.

industries.note: A ten-year guaranteed appropriation makes private detention, transport, and facility vendors the permanent funded channel for immigration enforcement, rather than vendors who must be re-selected each year. Their revenue grows as detention and enforcement expand, which runs against the interests of people subject to detention and taxpayers footing the bill.

The bill funds acquisition of additional real property, facility construction, and ongoing maintenance through 2036 — long-term contracts for builders and landowners near enforcement infrastructure. The bill leaves siting and standards to the agency, so communities hosting new facilities have little say.

Up to 3,790 police-type vehicles would be purchased or leased, a large order for automakers and fleet suppliers. This is a straightforward procurement with limited bearing on most people's lives beyond the cost to taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: A standalone ten-year appropriations bill on the Senate calendar with two cosponsors and no committee action is very unlikely to get its own floor vote. The more realistic path is that its funding priorities get folded into the annual Homeland Security appropriations bill or a broader spending package, where they would face negotiation — and where the ten-year lock-in and no-offset features would likely be stripped. If that happens, this bill's main legacy would be as a marker of the requested amounts.
